items.stem: Let y₁ = β₁ + β₂ + u₁; y₂ = 2β₁ + u₂; y₃ = β₁ − β₂ + u₃ with V(uᵢ) = σ², i = 1, 2, 3. Then the best linear unbiased estimators of β₁ and β₂ are respectively:
items.explanation: With X = [[1, 1], [2, 0], [1, −1]], X′X = [[6, 0], [0, 2]] and X′y = (y₁ + 2y₂ + y₃, y₁ − y₃)′. So β̂₁ = (y₁ + 2y₂ + y₃)/6 and β̂₂ = (y₁ − y₃)/2 — the divisors are 6 and 2, not 2 and 6. Official answer B. Response sheet Q105; you marked D — wrong.

items.stem: Consider two models  (I) yi = α + βxi + ui ; i = 1, 2, . . . n  (II) yi = α + βxi + γx2i + vi ; i = 1, 2, . . . n  Define A = (yi − a − bxi )2 , B = (yi − α̂ − β̂xi − γ̂x2i )2 where a and b are the least  P P squares estimates of α and β from model (I) and α̂, β̂ and γ̂ are the least square estimates of α, β and γ from model (II). Then which of the following is always correct?
options: It can happen that A = 0 but B ≤ 0
It can happen that B = 0 but A ≥ 0
